name: claude-code
description: Delegating a coding task to Claude Code in one of the owner's authorised project directories, and continuing its conversation across turns. Load when the work is inside a project the projects tool lists.

content.inline:
# Claude Code

Claude Code is a complete coding agent — it reads and edits files, runs
commands and git — working in one of the owner's **projects**: directories the
owner has authorised in Brightside's configuration. You never choose a
directory; the projects tool lists what you may use, and a task belongs to
exactly one of them.

## A turn

- run `{project, prompt, session?, model?, maxTurns?, allowedTools?, jsonSchema?}`
  does one turn as one job and returns `{result, session, turns, costUsd,
  permissionDenials, structured?}`. A turn can take minutes; that is normal.
- Give one complete, self-contained task per turn, with its acceptance
  criterion and what you want back: "Add a test for the retry path in
  Foo.java, run the module's tests, and report the outcome and the diff."
  Settle what you can with the owner first; if it still needs something
  decided, it ends its turn with the question, and you answer by continuing
  the session — taking it to the owner when it is theirs to decide.
- Do not paste file contents into the prompt; point at paths. It reads the
  project itself.
- Pass `session` from a previous result to continue that conversation with
  everything it already read, changed and concluded. Prefer that to
  re-explaining; start fresh for unrelated work. sessions lists what this
  venue knows; stop frees a live process (the conversation stays resumable).
- Bound exploration with `maxTurns`; a job that fails with error_max_turns
  names the session — resume it to let it finish. For a machine-readable
  answer pass `jsonSchema` and read `structured`.

## What it may do

What Claude Code may do is the project's setting, made by the owner. In
Brightside's own checkout the everyday developer tools — editing, building,
testing, package managers, git, looking around — are allowed outright, and
Claude Code's own safety checks judge anything else (moving data out,
deleting, the unusual); headless, nothing is ever waited on. A blocked action
comes back as a denial: report it, never work around it, and let the owner
decide whether to allow it. In another project the
owner may have set a permission mode and allowed tools; `permissionDenials`
in a result means it wanted a tool that project does not allow — say so
plainly, and if the owner wants it they widen the project's options in
config.json. You can narrow a turn (`allowedTools`, `maxTurns`) but never
widen it beyond the project.

## Reporting

`result` is its final message. Report it faithfully, including what it says it
could not do, and never claim work was done that the result does not confirm.
Anything outward-facing or hard to undo — pushing, publishing, deleting —
needs the owner's word before the turn that does it; the git skill has the
detail.
